These audits aimed to reduce energy costs by 17 to 34% and support efficient building operating practices as outlined in Akiachak’s Energy Action Plan (George et al. 2019). The goal was to use energy savings from initial retrofits to implement recommended improvements in other buildings, thereby increasing community resiliency and reducing reliance on fuel oil shipments. ANC has been steadily implementing energy efficiency measures based on previous audits of tribal buildings from 2017, with a primary objective of stabilizing and reducing energy costs. Understanding how a building performs regarding energy usage and cost is a key first step in determining efficiency improvement strategies. Tracking historic consumption and cost in relation to actual weather data allows a building owner to monitor changes in the facility’s performance or energy use. This data-driven approach helps to identify trends over time and pinpoint specific areas where energy consumption may be improved. ANC obtained energy audits for five buildings in 2017 and used them to guide this follow-up project, which focused on implementing high-payback recommendations such as replacing lighting with LEDs, installing programmable thermostats with setbacks, and air-tightening building envelopes. ANC and NREL expected to see reductions in building energy costs ranging from approximately 17% to 34%. These retrofits were intended to build on ANC’s long-term vision to support cost-effective building operations through energy efficiency. ANC anticipated outcomes from this project regarding high- payback, simple retrofits found in the energy audit process could be replicated with similar buildings in the village and region to avoid the time-delays and cost impacts from contracting energy audits. Other expected outcomes included increased energy resiliency and reduced dependence on imported fuel oil. The primary actors on the project were ANC, the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), Energy Audits of Alaska, and the Cold Climate Housing Research Center (CCHRC). As project lead, ANC made decisions on which building to prioritize, hosted vendors, and presented at OIE program reviews. NREL provided general project management, coordinated with the energy auditor to develop and administer RFPs, and coordinated travel for vendors flying to the village during implementation. NREL also gathered, analyzed, and reported project data, and assisted with quarterly progress and financial reporting.
